transcript.text: induction hob keeps turnin off after 5-10 mins on high, have to keep restartin it. drives me nuts. any1 know y?

That is not usually normal if the hob actually switches off and has to be restarted. The most likely reason is that its overheat protection is operating after several minutes at full power — commonly because ventilation is restricted or the cooling fan is not doing its job. Less commonly it is a temperature-sensor or control-board fault. A little power cycling on a high setting can be normal on some induction hobs, but a complete shut-down/restart requirement is not. 1. When the hob is cool, switch it off and isolate it at the cooker switch. Check that any visible ventilation openings around the worktop/cupboard area are not blocked by stored items, foil, towels or a drawer packed tightly underneath. Restricted airflow supports overheating.
2. Use a flat, magnetic pan with a base that matches the cooking zone, and avoid an empty pan or very small pan on maximum. If it only happens with one pan or one zone, that helps narrow it down.
3. When it cuts out, do all zones stop or only the one in use, and does the display show any letter/number or error symbol? All zones stopping points more towards whole-hob cooling or control; one zone points more towards that zone's sensor/power electronics. If the vents are clear and it still shuts down after 5–10 minutes, especially with all zones affected, it is likely to need an appliance engineer to check the cooling fan, thermal sensing and power electronics. Do not remove the hob or its covers yourself: induction hobs contain high-voltage components even after isolation.
mostly the big front zones when on high. fan roars b4 it cuts out. comes back after a few mins. started when new drawer unit was fitted last month, not doing anything under the hob tho

The timing with the new drawer unit makes restricted cooling airflow the leading suspect, even though nothing is stored in the drawer. The fan roaring suggests it is trying to remove heat; if the drawer carcass, back panel or a close-fitting divider has reduced the air space under the hob, the big front zones on high can overheat and shut themselves down until they cool. 1. With the hob cool and isolated at the cooker switch, open the drawer and inspect only what is visible: look for a solid drawer top, back panel, packing, foil insulation or a divider sitting very close to the underside of the hob or obstructing any ventilation space. Don’t remove the hob or panels. If there is little/no open air space, ask the kitchen fitter to check the hob manufacturer’s required ventilation clearances. 2. As a simple comparison, use the same pan on a rear zone, or use a smaller suitable magnetic pan on a front zone at high power. If the front zones still cut out much sooner, it supports a heat build-up issue around those zones; if it happens only with one particular large pan, the pan/load is contributing. If the visible clearances look reasonable and it still happens across different pans, an engineer should check the cooling fan airflow, thermal sensor and power electronics; induction hobs should not be dismantled by the owner.
not pulling the drawer out or lookin under the hob, not my thing. tried same pans on the rear zones? no, i use high a lot on the front ones. so what do i do, call someone?

Yes — call the kitchen fitter first, rather than an appliance repair firm. Because it began after the drawer unit was fitted, the most likely issue is that the new furniture has reduced the ventilation space beneath or behind the hob. The roaring fan and recovery after a few minutes fit the hob protecting itself from overheating. Ask the fitter to check the installation against the hob manufacturer’s ventilation-clearance requirements, including the space above the drawer, any drawer top/back panel, and the airflow route in and out of the cabinet. They do not need to alter the electrical parts of the hob to assess the cabinet ventilation. If the fitter suggests the required clearances are present and nothing is obstructing airflow, then book an appliance engineer to investigate cooling-fan airflow, temperature sensing or the power electronics. Until it is checked, avoid repeatedly running the front zones flat-out for long periods. Stop using it and arrange urgent help if there is a burning smell, smoke, sparking, or a persistent error display.

candidates: Overheating protection from restricted ventilation or a cooling fan problem (high)
A temperature sensor or electronic control fault (medium)
Pan/base or high-power operating conditions causing the zone to reduce output (low)
